title: Pipeline Panic

coach.board: The board shows your pipeline (or your release) and the next event it will face, before it happens.
coach.actions: Place, remove or promote to change the pipeline. Run next event or Wait lets time pass and shows the result.
coach.firstMove: Read the next event on the board, then place or promote the one thing that answers it before you run it.

lossRule: Delivery health fell below the floor: too many slow, unsafe or failed releases got through.

events.title: A docs-only PR runs the whole suite
events.fix: on.<event>.paths and paths-ignore decide whether the whole workflow runs at all. Skip it when only Markdown and docs change, and the minutes are never spent.

events.title: Every run downloads the dependencies again
events.fix: Key a cache on a hash of the lockfile (or use the cache: input of setup-node) so installs only repeat when the dependencies change.

events.title: A PR fails lint, and the full test suite runs anyway
events.fix: Jobs run in parallel by default. needs: lint makes the test job wait for lint and skip itself when lint fails, so a PR that cannot merge costs one minute.

events.title: Five pushes to one PR in a minute
events.fix: Without concurrency every push starts its own full run. A concurrency group per branch with cancel-in-progress keeps only the newest run.

events.title: A change that only breaks on Node 18
events.fix: A single-version job only proves the change on that version. strategy.matrix runs one job per version, so the failure shows up before merge, at the price of more minutes.

events.title: The same lint job is copy-pasted into four workflows
events.fix: A reusable workflow (workflow_call) is a whole set of jobs, called with uses: ./.github/workflows/x.yml. Change it once and every caller follows.

events.title: The same three setup steps are pasted into every job
events.fix: A composite action reuses a handful of steps inside an existing job, on the same runner, without a whole extra job. Check the repository out first, then call it.

events.title: A fork PR tries to read your secrets
events.fix: pull_request from a fork runs with a read-only token and no secrets. pull_request_target runs with them, so it must never check out and run the PR's own code. The trigger alone is not the danger: privileged context plus untrusted code is.

events.title: A fork PR with a failing test is not tested
events.fix: pull_request_target checks out the base branch by default, so the PR's code never runs and the check goes green for nothing. Test fork PRs with pull_request, which is safe by default.

events.title: A third-party action is compromised upstream
events.fix: A branch like @main moves whenever upstream pushes, and a tag can be moved too. A full commit SHA cannot be repointed, so pin third-party actions to one.

events.title: A dependency tries to push to the repo with the job token
events.fix: Scope GITHUB_TOKEN to what the job needs: permissions: contents: read for CI. Widen it per job only where a job really writes.

events.title: A bad release is rolling out
events.fix: A rolling deployment replaces pods in batches, so the errors grow with every batch before anyone can react. Rolling back is another rollout, one batch at a time.

events.title: A bad release took 100% of traffic at the cutover
events.fix: Blue-green sends all traffic to the new version at once: a big spike. The rollback is the strength: flip the router back and the old version is serving again instantly.

events.title: The canary slice shows errors
events.fix: A canary exposes a small slice of real traffic first. The graph shows the problem while only about 5% of users are affected, and aborting shifts the weight back to 0%.

events.title: Smoke tests failed on the idle green environment
events.fix: Blue-green lets you run smoke tests against the new environment directly before any user is routed to it. Tearing it down costs nobody anything.

events.title: Staging caught the bug
events.fix: Each environment adds confidence before the next. A red staging soak is the gate doing its job: reject the release and prod never sees it.

events.title: A release skipped staging and the bug reached prod
events.fix: Promotion goes dev, staging, prod for a reason. Skipping or overriding the staging gate removes the cheapest place to find a bug.

events.title: A migration drops a column the running version still reads
events.fix: During a rollout old and new versions run side by side, so the schema must work for both: adding a column is safe, dropping one needs the code to stop using it in an earlier release (expand, then contract). After a destructive migration there is nothing to roll back to.

events.title: Someone hot-fixed prod by hand
events.fix: The cluster no longer matches git, and the next deploy silently reverts the patch. With GitOps the repo is the source of truth: commit the change and let the operator reconcile, instead of applying it from a laptop.

on-push.label: on: push (main)
on-push.tip: Runs on every push to main.

on-pr.label: on: pull_request
on-pr.tip: Runs on PRs. From a fork it gets a read-only token and no secrets.

on-prt.label: on: pull_request_target
on-prt.tip: Runs in the base repo's context: secrets and a write token are available.

on-schedule.label: on: schedule (nightly)
on-schedule.tip: A cron run every night: it bills a full run each event.

paths-ignore.label: paths-ignore: **.md, docs/**
paths-ignore.tip: Skip the workflow when only these files change.

cache-setup.label: setup-node with cache: npm
cache-setup.tip: The built-in cache input of setup-node.

matrix.label: strategy.matrix: node 18, 20
matrix.tip: One test job per Node version: twice the minutes.

needs-lint.label: test needs: lint
needs-lint.tip: The test job waits for lint, and is skipped if lint fails.

concurrency.label: concurrency: cancel-in-progress
concurrency.tip: One run per branch; a newer push cancels the older run.

perms-read.label: permissions: contents: read
perms-read.tip: Least privilege for the job token.

ref-main.label: notify-slack@main
ref-main.tip: A branch ref: it moves whenever upstream pushes.

ref-tag.label: notify-slack@v2
ref-tag.tip: A tag ref: readable, but a tag can be moved.

ref-sha.label: notify-slack@<full commit SHA>
ref-sha.tip: A full commit SHA: it cannot be repointed.

reusable-lint.label: lint: uses reusable-lint.yml
reusable-lint.tip: Call the reusable workflow (workflow_call) instead of pasting the lint job.

composite-setup.label: setup: composite action
composite-setup.tip: Fold the setup steps into a composite action, called after checkout.

checkout-head.label: checkout the PR head (ref: head.sha)
checkout-head.tip: Check out the pull request's own code instead of the base branch.

levels.title: 1. Fast feedback
levels.blurb: Pipeline Tycoon. The team ships through one slow workflow. Add cards so each PR gets fast feedback without burning the monthly runner minutes. The next event is shown before you run it.
hints: Look at the event shown before each run: it names the cost you are about to pay (minutes, a cache miss, a slow job).
Docs-only changes, reinstalled dependencies, jobs that run one after another and old runs that keep going all burn minutes.
Place paths-ignore, cache-setup, needs-lint, concurrency and matrix, then run the next event.
lessons: Skip work that cannot change the result: paths-ignore for docs-only changes, a dependency cache, and concurrency to cancel runs a newer push has replaced.
Run independent jobs in parallel, use needs only where order matters, and fan tests out with a matrix.

tryItForReal.needs: a GitHub repository with Actions enabled
tryItForReal.commands:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
on:
  pull_request:
    paths-ignore: ['**.md', 'docs/**']
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [18, 20, 22]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci && npm test

levels.title: 2. Locked down
levels.blurb: Pipeline Tycoon. Someone switched the workflow to pull_request_target to get secrets into fork builds. Make it safe, pin what you do not control, and stop the copy-paste before the next fork PR arrives.
hints: Look at the red cards in the workflow: the trigger and the checkout.
pull_request_target runs with secrets, and checking out the fork's head code in it is the dangerous pair.
Remove on-prt and checkout-head, place on-pr, perms-read and ref-sha, then the reusable-lint and composite-setup cards.
lessons: pull_request_target runs with the base repository's secrets, so never check out and run a fork's code in it: use pull_request for untrusted code.
Give the token the least it needs (permissions: contents: read), pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA, and move repeated steps into a reusable workflow or composite action.

tryItForReal.needs: a GitHub repository with Actions enabled
tryItForReal.commands:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
on: pull_request            # not pull_request_target
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  lint:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-lint.yml
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>   # pin, do not use a moving tag
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup              # a composite action for the shared steps
      - run: npm test

levels.title: 3. Deploy Day
levels.blurb: Deploy Day. Three releases wait in dev. Promote each through staging, then pick rolling, blue-green or canary for prod. Watch the error graph and roll back before users notice. Keep delivery health at 70 or more.
hints: Watch the error graph while a release bakes: the strategies differ in how many users see a bad build.
Rolling replaces pods gradually, canary sends a few users first, blue-green flips everyone at once with an instant way back.
Promote to staging and wait, then pick a strategy; the riskier the release, the smaller the first step. Roll back as soon as errors climb.
lessons: Rolling swaps pods gradually, a canary shows a bad build to a few users first, and blue-green keeps the old version running for an instant switch back.
Watch the error rate while a release bakes, and roll back first: diagnose after the users are safe.

levels.title: 4. Gates and drift
levels.blurb: Deploy Day. A release that staging would catch, someone hot-fixing prod by hand, and a migration that drops a column. Use the gates, keep prod matching git, and never ship a change you cannot undo.
hints: Look at each release before you promote it: the gates are there for builds staging would catch.
Three traps: a release staging would reject, a hot-fix made by hand in prod, and a migration that drops a column.
Reject the bad build, expand the schema before removing anything, commit the hand-fix to git, deploy with a canary and roll back if it fails.
path: Expand the schema first (add before you remove)
lessons: A gate only helps if a bad release stops at it: reject before prod, and keep prod matching git by committing any hand-fix.
Make a column change in steps: expand (add), migrate and deploy, then contract (drop), so you can always undo the last step.
